ranking.reasoning: GS revenue growth should revert toward high-single-digit/mid-single-digit norms after an unusually strong recent run driven by trading/IB recovery and asset management growth, with capital markets cyclicality as the main swing factor. Net margin is expected to settle near its TTM/5Y average (~15-17%) as elevated recent profitability normalizes, though efficiency gains and buybacks support stable returns; the main risk is a capital markets downturn or regulatory capital requirements compressing margins and growth.

BAC's revenue growth will likely normalize toward low-single-digit rates tied to loan growth, net interest margin trends, and fee income, after the recent YoY spike (driven by base effects and trading/NII recovery) fades. Net margin should revert toward its historical 28-30% range as credit costs normalize and rate tailwinds moderate, with key risks being a sharp yield curve inversion, credit deterioration, or regulatory capital changes compressing margins.

JPM's revenue growth will likely normalize from current elevated TTM figures (distorted by rate environment and trading/IB rebound) toward historical mid-single-digit rates driven by loan growth, fee income, and modest NII expansion, though a recessionary or sharp rate-cutting scenario could flatten growth. Net margins should revert toward the 28-30% historical norm as net interest margins normalize from cyclically high levels and credit costs normalize upward from current benign levels. Main risks are credit cycle turns, regulatory capital requirements, and net interest margin compression if

Disney's growth drivers are streaming profitability (Disney+/Hulu reaching scale economics), parks pricing power, and cost-cutting under Iger/D'Amaro, offset by linear TV secular decline and cord-cutting pressuring the Media Networks segment. Base case assumes low-to-mid single digit revenue growth with margins recovering toward historical ~10-13% net margin as streaming losses turn to profit, though content spend inflation and macro-sensitive consumer discretionary spending (parks) are key risks to both tails.

UNH remains the largest US health insurer/PBM with steady Medicare Advantage and Optum growth, but 2024-2025 margin compression from elevated medical cost ratios, DOJ/CalPERS litigation overhangs, and regulatory scrutiny on MA reimbursement create downside risk to both growth and profitability. Base case assumes gradual margin recovery toward historical ~5% net margin as cost trends normalize and pricing catches up, with revenue growth moderating to high-single digits as the company scales off a ~$400B base; upside depends on successful Optum expansion and MA stabilization, downside on sustain

Pfizer faces a patent cliff on legacy products and fading COVID franchise revenue, but cost-cutting, pipeline launches (vaccines, oncology from Seagen, eczema/dermatology assets) and new product cycles should support modest single-digit growth after stabilization. Margins are currently depressed by one-time items and COVID inventory writedowns/impairments, so normalization plus cost savings programs should restore net margins toward historical double-digit levels, though generic competition and R&D/launch costs remain key risks.

Netflix's growth is decelerating from historical teens-rates toward high-single/low-double digits as subscriber penetration matures in core markets, with ads tier, password-sharing crackdown and price increases providing continued but slowing upside; live sports/events are a wildcard driver. Margins should stay well above the historical streaming-industry norm given scale and operating leverage, but intensifying competition from YouTube, Paramount/WBD consolidation, and content cost inflation cap further expansion, so margins likely plateau near current levels rather than continuing to rise sh

Oracle's OCI and RPO backlog (fueled by large AI/cloud deals like Tencent) support above-trend growth for a company of its size, but massive capex for data centers and AI infrastructure plus rising debt load are compressing near-term margins. Base rate reversion suggests growth decelerates from current elevated 20%+ YoY rates toward low-teens over 5 years, with net margin settling below the TTM peak as depreciation and interest costs from the capex buildout weigh on profitability; key risk is execution/competition from AWS/Azure/GCP in the AI cloud race.

Salesforce's growth has decelerated to low double digits as it matures and faces competitive pressure in CRM/SaaS from AI-native entrants, with Agentforce and AI monetization offering upside but large-enterprise IT budget cyclicality posing downside risk. Margins should continue expanding modestly from cost discipline and operating leverage but will likely plateau as reinvestment in AI and competitive pricing pressure offset further gains, settling near current TTM levels rather than expanding indefinitely. Main risk: slower enterprise software spend growth and AI disruption compressing both g

Home Depot's growth should track modest housing turnover, home price appreciation, and Pro/SRS expansion, with low-single-digit CAGR as the base case given mature US market saturation and recent soft comps from weak discretionary remodel demand; upside depends on housing market recovery and continued M&A (SRS) integration, while downside risk comes from prolonged high rates suppressing existing home sales and big-ticket renovations. Margins are likely to stay near current levels (~8-9% net margin) as mix shift toward lower-margin Pro/supply chain investments offsets operating leverage, reverti

Meta's core ad business still benefits from AI-driven targeting/engagement gains and scale (27-28% recent YoY growth), but base effects, ad-market saturation, and competition (TikTok, YouTube) should decelerate growth toward high-single/low-double digits over five years. Net margins likely compress modestly from current ~30% as heavy capex/opex for AI infrastructure and Reality Labs losses weigh on profitability, though still above typical media-industry norms given Meta's dominant ad efficiency. Main risk: capex intensity from AI buildout fails to generate proportional revenue, compressing ma

NVIDIA's AI/datacenter demand remains strong near-term, but current TTM revenue growth (~83%) and net margins (~64%) are far above sustainable base rates and will likely revert as the AI capex cycle matures, competition (AMD, custom ASICs, hyperscaler in-house chips) intensifies, and the law of large numbers constrains growth off a ~$130B+ revenue base. Main risk is a sharp AI-spending slowdown or share loss compressing both growth and margins faster than the median case assumes, while upside case assumes AI infrastructure buildout continues multi-year without major disruption.

Azure and AI-driven cloud demand should keep Microsoft growing well above typical large-cap rates, but massive capex for AI infrastructure and intensifying competition from Google, Amazon, and OpenAI-related ecosystems could compress incremental margins and growth durability. Net margin is expected to stay elevated versus tech peers given software mix and scale, but likely reverts slightly from current record highs as depreciation from AI capex and competitive pricing pressure weigh on profitability.

XOM revenue is heavily tied to oil/gas price cycles and refining margins, so growth will largely track commodity prices rather than organic volume gains, with Guyana and Permian production providing modest structural upside. Net margin should revert toward its historical 8-10% norm as current elevated downstream/upstream spreads normalize, with integrated model and cost discipline supporting stability. Main risk is oil price volatility and energy transition pressures, which could swing both revenue and margins significantly in either direction.

Mastercard's growth is driven by continued cross-border volume recovery, secular cash-to-card/digital payment conversion, and value-added services expansion, though current mid-teens growth is elevated versus its historical ~10-12% base rate and should moderate as comps normalize and macro consumer spending growth slows. Main risks are regulatory/interchange pressure (EU digital euro, antitrust actions) and stablecoin/real-time payment rails disintermediating card networks; margins should stay near current best-in-class levels but face slight reversion from elevated TTM highs due to continued

Visa's scale, network effects, and secular cash-to-digital conversion support continued high-single to low-double-digit revenue growth, though recent 14%+ growth likely moderates as the base grows and cash-displacement opportunity matures. Margins should stay near current elevated levels given asset-light model and operating leverage, with main risks being stablecoin/real-time payment disincentermediation, regulatory/interchange pressure, and macro-driven consumer spending slowdowns.

Growth driven by continued Search/YouTube ad strength, Cloud scaling toward profitability, and AI-driven product expansion, though current TTM revenue growth (~20%) is unlikely to persist at that pace over five years given base-rate reversion and increasing competition from AI-native alternatives. Net margin is forecast to revert toward the high-20s from the current unusually elevated TTM level (54.77%, inflated by one-time items/investment gains), consistent with heavy AI capex, regulatory/antitrust risk, and normalized operating margins in the high-20s to low-30s range. Main risks: antitrust

Chevron's revenue is heavily tied to oil/gas price cycles, so growth will largely track commodity prices rather than organic volume gains, with Hess integration adding some production upside; base case assumes modest price-driven growth near historical energy-sector averages. Net margin should revert toward its 5-10yr historical norm (~9-10%) as refining/chemicals normalize and upstream margins stay cyclical, with downside risk from a prolonged oil price slump and upside from supply constraints or geopolitical premiums.

Boeing is recovering from production and certification issues, with 737 MAX rate increases, a resolved labor contract, and strong defense orders supporting mid-single-digit to double-digit revenue growth over five years as deliveries normalize and backlog converts to revenue. Margins should improve from today's thin levels as fixed-price defense program losses fade and commercial volume leverage returns, but execution risk, supply chain constraints, and historically weak defense program profitability keep upside margin limited near historical industry norms (~5-6%).

AWS and advertising growth plus operating leverage support high-single to low-double-digit revenue CAGR, though a ~$2.7T base makes sustained double-digit growth harder and retail/cloud competition (Azure, Google Cloud, Walmart) caps upside. Net margin should moderate from the current TTM 17.4% (boosted by investment gains and cost cuts) back toward a more sustainable 9-11% as capex for AI/logistics normalizes and e-commerce margins stay thin, with risk of margin compression from heavy AI infrastructure spend or macro-driven consumer weakness.

JNJ's growth is driven by MedTech expansion and new pharma launches (Darzalex, Tremfya, Rybrevant) offsetting Stelara biosimilar erosion, with base-rate large-pharma growth in low-to-mid single digits; recent 6-8% YoY growth likely moderates as patent cliffs and generic competition bite. Net margin should settle below the elevated historical ~27-29% levels toward the mid-20s as legal costs (talc litigation), R&D intensity, and pricing pressure persist, while still benefiting from scale and mix shift to higher-margin MedTech/Innovative Medicine. Main risk: litigation overhangs and faster-than-e

Apple's growth will likely be driven by Services expansion, continued installed-base monetization, and new categories (AI-enabled devices, health features), but iPhone hardware growth remains structurally low-single-digit given market saturation. Margins should stay near current elevated levels due to Services mix shift offsetting hardware commoditization, with main risks being regulatory/antitrust pressure on Services fees, China competition/demand softness, and supply chain or tariff disruptions.

Walmart's revenue growth has been running 5-6% recently driven by grocery share gains, e-commerce/advertising/membership growth, and international expansion, but base effects and market saturation make reversion toward low-to-mid single digits likely over five years. Margins should see modest expansion from high-margin ad/membership/marketplace revenue mix and automation, but intense grocery price competition (Kroger, Aldi, Costco) and potential tariff/inflation cost pressure cap upside, keeping net margin near historical 3% norm with slight improvement.

Caterpillar is a cyclical capital goods company; recent double-digit growth reflects a strong infrastructure/data-center-driven upcycle plus pricing, but machinery demand is historically mean-reverting and sensitive to construction, mining, and energy capex cycles. Base rate suggests mid-single-digit CAGR over five years with a wide range given cyclicality, while margins should settle near the high end of its historical 13-15% range as operating leverage and services mix offset cyclical pricing pressure. Main risk: a global industrial/construction downturn or mining capex pullback that compres

AMD's data-center GPU/CPU share gains (MI300/MI350 ramp, EPYC share vs Intel) and AI accelerator demand support strong growth, with margins improving from operating leverage and datacenter mix, though still below Nvidia-level profitability due to competitive pricing. Main risks are cyclicality in PC/gaming, intense competition from Nvidia/Intel/custom silicon, and potential AI capex slowdown that could compress both growth and margins toward low-single-digit/legacy semiconductor norms in a downside scenario.

Tesla's growth has decelerated sharply (TTM 11.75% vs 5Y 24.63%) amid EV demand softness and intensifying competition from BYD and other low-cost entrants, but new catalysts (robotaxi, energy storage, robotics/Optimus) could reaccelerate growth if commercialized successfully. Margins are likely to stay below past peaks given pricing pressure and heavy R&D/capex spend, though improving scale, software/services mix, and potential robotaxi high-margin revenue support gradual margin recovery. Main risk: execution failure on autonomy/robotics bets combined with continued price wars could keep growt

Intel's revenue has been volatile (5Y CAGR negative) but recent quarterly growth and AI-driven demand plus foundry ramp provide upside; base case assumes modest single-digit growth as PC/server markets stabilize and foundry business scales. Margins should recover from current deeply negative TTM levels as cost cuts, capex discipline, and foundry utilization improve, but intense competition from TSMC, AMD, and Nvidia in both design and manufacturing caps upside and is the key risk to both growth and margin durability.

changeLog.text: Fixed a second crypto data bug: the agent was judging each coin on the current, barely started daily bar (about an hour of trading). It now uses the last completed day.

Fixed a data bug: the nightly crypto agent had only been receiving prices for XRP (one of its 10 coins), so it never found a trade. It now sees all 10. Crypto results before this date reflect the bug.

Started a separate long-horizon track: Claude forecasts company fundamentals, code ranks them, and a virtual top-5 portfolio is tracked against SPY. It places no orders and doesn't touch the nightly strategy.
Added a kill switch, a clean-run log, and a dry-run of a $30 live account. Nothing about which trades get made changed.
Shorts now need a specific, stated reason, and the agent is no longer forced to make 3-5 picks a night. Shorts had been the main source of losses.
The direction hit rate is now checked against real prices. Claude's own, more generous grade is shown separately.
Every trade is now compared with simply holding SPY over the same window.
Positions now close by their own share count, with guards so different strategies can't net against each other.
Kept short-side sizing unchanged despite weak results, to avoid acting twice on the same small sample.
Position size is cut in half for low confidence, upcoming events, and shorts, based on the system's own results.
Claude started rating its own confidence on each pick.
Simulated trades can be long or short.

lessons.lessonText: All 11 trades here are "watch whether X extends/continues" framings riding on someone else's cited catalyst (analyst upgrade, sector peer news, macro data point) rather than a primary, firm-specific data event — and all 11 lost, regardless of long/short or confidence. Worth weighing: second-hand narrative catalysts (Ives grouping AAPL with AI names, Cramer citing SpaceX/GPUs, "sector also rallying" framing for JNJ/HD/CAT) may be weaker signals than they appear, since they're sentiment-echo rather than company-specific fundamentals. Also notable: eventRisk=false dominates this batch (9 of 11) yet losses were still frequent and sometimes large (CAT -4.17%, NVDA -2.03%, CRM -2.21%), suggesting the eventRisk flag as currently set isn't capturing the actual risk driving these losses. Sample is small and single-themed (mostly AI/industrial momentum names in one week), so treat this as a narrow pattern, not a general rule.
Shorting stocks that already fell sharply the same day (AMZN -2.2%, GOOGL -3.81%, ORCL -3.1%

Momentum-continuation bets ("watch whether X extends") dominate this batch and lose regardless of direction — both longs chasing a rally and shorts chasing a selloff failed repeatedly (CAT, INTC, ORCL, GS, NVDA, XOM, GOOGL), suggesting the "continuation vs. fade" framing itself isn't adding edge here.

Trades explicitly noting low or below-average volume confirming the move (CAT, INTC x2, ORCL, TSLA) still lost, including some big misses (INTC -6.89%, -5.97%), so "weak volume, likely to fade/reverse" is not a reliable signal in this sample.

Pre-earnings or event-adjacent theses (CRM, ORCL x3, NVDA, AMD) produced some of the largest losses (CRM -15.59%, ORCL -5.99%, -3.90%), hinting that positioning ahead of scheduled catalysts carries outsized tail risk regardless of confidence label.

No clear pattern tied to the confidence field itself — medium and unrated trades both lost similarly, so confidence as recorded doesn't appear predictive here.
